text: PLPC should be promoted to the primary underfollowed candidate for the transmission-line hardware node, pending verification through filings, utility approved-vendor lists and project procurement documents.

HUBB is the large-cap reference product leader for transmission connectors, insulators, arresters, anchors and related utility hardware, but is less suitable for underfollowed alpha discovery due to size and broader coverage.
VMI is an adjacent underfollowed infrastructure supplier through transmission and substation structures, not a pure clamps/fittings/conductor-hardware name.

PWR is a demand/customer anchor for the node: EPC transmission awards and line-mile construction should be monitored as leading indicators for hardware suppliers rather than treated as direct manufacturing exposure.

Need a follow-up search for smaller public or foreign-listed suppliers of OPGW fittings, dead-ends, splices, clamps, pole-line hardware, substation connectors and utility-approved conductor accessories; many likely competitors are private or embedded inside conglomerates.
PLPC should be carried forward as the highest-priority underfollowed direct candidate for transmission-line hardware, fittings, clamps, anchors, splices, and OPGW-adjacent hardware.
HUBB should be retained as the reference benchmark, especially after DMC Power added high-voltage connector and tooling exposure for utility substation and transmission markets.

NVT is a second-order utility connection/protection candidate via ERICO grounding, bonding, lightning protection, and utility connector products; evidence needed on revenue mix and approved utility specifications.
AZZ is a second-order materials/capacity candidate via hot-dip galvanizing for utility T&D steel; keep as underfollowed but require revenue-mix and customer evidence before upgrading.
Need primary evidence for utility approved-vendor lists, product requalification cycles, lead times, and whether transmission hardware/fittings face capacity constraints versus generic demand growth.

PLPC should be carried forward as the primary underfollowed candidate for the transmission-line hardware node because its product catalog and external research directly match clamps, dead-ends, OPGW hardware, anchoring/control hardware, and utility-qualified line components.

HUBB should be retained as a reference benchmark, not the main underfollowed lane, because Hubbell Power Systems has direct transmission connector and fitting overlap but the company is much larger and broader.
AZZ is a second-order underfollowed candidate for coatings/galvanizing of T&D structures and components; survival in later layers depends on quantifying utility/T&D revenue exposure.
VMI is an adjacent transmission-structures reference name rather than a direct fittings/clamps candidate; use it to benchmark utility transmission capex and lead-time evidence.

The node appears investable through three public-market mappings: direct line hardware suppliers, broader connector/fitting incumbents, and second-order structure/coating suppliers tied to the same transmission BOM.

Need targeted verification of utility approved-vendor lists, project specifications, customer concentration, and product-level revenue because public company segment labels often obscure the exact transmission-line hardware exposure.

PLPC should be treated as the highest-purity US-listed candidate for the transmission_line_hardware node; next layer should verify utility-spec inclusion, revenue mix, backlog, and high-voltage exposure.
HUBB is a useful reference comparator for utility connectors/fittings but is too diversified and higher-attention to be the primary underfollowed discovery expression.

VMI belongs in an adjacent chokepoint lane for engineered transmission structures rather than conductor fittings; useful if the funnel broadens from hardware/fittings to the full transmission-line BOM.

AZZ is an underfollowed adjacent-process candidate: hot-dip galvanizing for utility transmission/distribution steel may benefit from grid capex, but it must be separated from general construction/industrial cyclicality.

Need targeted searches for US-listed OPGW hardware, dead-end/splice manufacturers, substation connector specialists, utility-approved clamp/fitting distributors, and public subsidiaries hidden inside diversified industrials.

HUBB should remain a reference anchor for data-center PDU transformers and dry-type power distribution products, but its large market cap and broad exposure make it less suitable for the underfollowed lane.

POWL is highly relevant to electrical rooms, switchgear, and power-control systems adjacent to transformers, but current market cap and strong rerating reduce its fit as a fresh underfollowed small/mid-cap discovery.

BELFB is a plausible underfollowed mid-cap hypothesis for power/magnetics exposure; survival in later layers requires proof that Power and Magnetic Solutions growth is tied to data centers, industrial electrification, or grid infrastructure.
ESP is a direct custom magnetics and transformer micro-cap exception, but current evidence maps mainly to defense/rugged industrial markets; data-center/electrification linkage is unproven.

The cleanest North American dry-type transformer pure-play from provided context is Hammond Power Solutions, but primary listing is not US; a separate non-US/OTC pass should decide whether to track it as a benchmark or excluded asset.

For this node, direct investable exposure should not be limited to transformer manufacturers; electrical houses, PDU transformers, switchgear-adjacent control systems, custom magnetics, power conversion, and UPS/power-quality systems all deserve Layer 2 verification.
POWL should be tracked as a US-listed data-center power-distribution and medium-voltage switchgear beneficiary, but not as a pure dry-type transformer supplier.
BELFB is a lower-attention US-listed candidate for custom magnetics and data-center power conversion; materiality to AI/data-center revenue remains the key evidence gap.

PPSI is a below-$300M speculative exception with node relevance through packaged electrical distribution, switchgear and medium-voltage transformer-integrated E-Bloc systems; execution and scale risks are high.

Hammond Power Solutions appears highly relevant to the node but is TSX-listed rather than a primary US exchange listing; keep as a non-US-listed benchmark/pure-play reference for later relative analysis.

POWL should be retained as the U.S.-listed reference anchor for engineered power-distribution packages, especially data-center medium-voltage switchgear, e-houses and power-control rooms; attention level is no longer low after the 2026 backlog/order rerating.

ESE is a strong underfollowed candidate for the testing/diagnostics gate of the transformer and grid-equipment cycle through Doble and Megger, with exposure hidden inside a diversified industrial profile.

ATKR is a second-order electrical-infrastructure supplier to data centers and electrification projects through conduit, fittings and cable-management products; verify pricing-cycle noise before advancing.

PPSI is a micro-cap speculative exception only; advance only if filings show material signed orders for PRYMUS or critical-power systems tied to data centers, industrial electrification or grid-constrained customers.

The purest dry-type transformer candidate found in provided context is Hammond Power Solutions, but it is Canada-listed/OTC rather than a primary U.S.-listed equity; a separate non-U.S. or OTC pass should evaluate HPS.A/HMDPF and peers.
POWL should be retained as a reference electrical-room/switchgear name, but not treated as underfollowed after its visible $1.8B backlog and $400M+ data-center order disclosure.

HMDPF/HPS.A is the cleanest direct public mapping found for dry-type transformers, power-quality products, and custom magnetics, but US investors must verify OTC liquidity and primary TSX listing constraints.
BELFB is a plausible underfollowed magnetics/power-conversion candidate; survival in later layers depends on proving AI/data-center networking linkage rather than generic networking cyclicality.

PLPC belongs in an adjacent chokepoint watchlist for grid/transmission hardware rather than the core transformer node; evidence must verify incremental pull-through from data-center interconnection and utility capex.

Need a follow-up pass for other US-listed smaller electrical equipment suppliers: remanufactured transformers, harmonic filters, power-factor correction, electrical enclosures/rooms, testing/certification, and distributor-mediated transformer bottlenecks.

AMSC is the cleanest US-listed underfollowed direct candidate for the HVDC/FACTS/grid-stability node because its D-VAR product is explicitly a STATCOM/FACTS-adjacent reactive-power and voltage-control solution.

PLPC is a strong underfollowed second-order transmission-hardware candidate, but direct HVDC/FACTS component exposure is not yet proven and must be verified through project/customer/specification evidence.
HUBB is a large-cap component/platform candidate with instrument-transformer and substation apparatus exposure; include only if later layers accept less pure but still component-level grid exposure.
GEV should be retained as the reference OEM/system-integrator anchor for mapping component suppliers, but not as the main underfollowed alpha candidate.

US-listed universe lacks many pure HVDC reactor/filter/instrument-transformer specialists; external context points to non-US-listed India/Canada/Europe suppliers, so a later international pass should expand beyond US listings.
AMSC is the highest-priority US-listed underfollowed candidate for this node because D-VAR is directly mapped to STATCOM/reactive-power/grid-stability use cases.

PLPC should remain in the Layer 1 universe as a second-order transmission-hardware candidate, but survival depends on evidence of high-voltage project exposure, utility qualification stickiness, or HVDC/substation linkage.
POWL is a speculative-shadow candidate for FACTS/HVDC balance-of-plant and utility/industrial electrical-control infrastructure; direct node evidence is currently weak.
GE Vernova is the reference anchor for HVDC/FACTS/STATCOM/reactor/capacitor mapping and should be used to identify subsystem suppliers rather than as the main underfollowed alpha target.

The strongest pure-play evidence for reactors, harmonic filters, instrument transformers, STATCOM-adjacent components, and HVDC/FACTS customer wins appears to include non-US-listed companies such as India's Quality Power Electrical Equipments; US-listed equivalents may be scarce or hidden in broader industrials.

AMSC is the cleanest US-listed underfollowed candidate for the FACTS/STATCOM portion of the HVDC/FACTS/grid-stability node; verify current grid-segment revenue, D-VAR backlog, and utility/renewable order cadence in latest filings.

PLPC is a small-cap transmission/substation hardware candidate with strong second-order grid-buildout relevance, but direct HVDC/FACTS linkage is unproven and must be verified through product specs, utility standards, and project references.

POWL belongs in the underfollowed second-order lane because its engineered substations, E-Houses, switchgear, and control systems overlap utility/industrial electrification; direct HVDC/FACTS customer exposure remains an evidence gap.
GE Vernova should be used as a reference anchor and supplier-map source for this node, not as the alpha-hunting target, because it is a mega-cap high-attention direct grid leader.

US-listed pure-play suppliers of HVDC reactors, harmonic filters, and instrument transformers appear scarce from this pass; many purer component suppliers may be non-US-listed, private, or embedded inside larger OEMs.
AMSC is the strongest US-listed underfollowed direct candidate for the FACTS/STATCOM portion of the HVDC/FACTS/grid-stability node; prioritize latest filings and order cadence verification.

PLPC is a plausible second-order high-voltage transmission hardware beneficiary, but direct HVDC/FACTS exposure is unproven and should be verified through voltage-class catalogs, utility specs and project references.

POWL is adjacent to the node through utility/industrial power distribution and control systems; include only as a hypothesis until direct HVDC converter-station, FACTS substation or grid-stability project exposure is found.
GEV should remain the reference anchor for mapping smaller US-listed suppliers because it directly offers HVDC, FACTS, SVC and STATCOM systems.

Need a follow-up search for US-listed or US-OTC niche suppliers of instrument transformers, harmonic filters, reactors, capacitors, insulators, arresters, thyristors/IGBT valves, control software and testing/commissioning services tied to HVDC/FACTS projects.
LEU is the highest-purity US-listed enrichment/HALEU candidate for this node; key survival test is funded commercial-scale capacity, not just licensing or DOE eligibility.

XE is a newly public 2026 fuel-fabrication discovery candidate; its TRISO-X NRC Part 70 HALEU fuel-fabrication license makes it more directly relevant to the node than a generic SMR screen would show.
LTBR should remain speculative_shadow until irradiation testing, pilot-fabrication funding, licensing path, and customer adoption are materially de-risked.

Cameco/CCJ is a major US-listed conversion reference via Port Hope and Westinghouse exposure, but because it is large-cap and high-attention in uranium, later layers should compare it separately against purer US enrichment/fabrication names.

DOE HALEU deconversion awardees also include Framatome, GE Vernova, Orano, Westinghouse, BWXT, and Centrus; several are private, foreign/state-owned, or diversified, so public-market exposure may be indirect.
LEU should remain the primary underfollowed direct candidate for the US-listed HALEU/enrichment lane; later layers must separate legacy fuel-services revenue from scalable HALEU economics.
BWXT belongs in the reference lane for HALEU deconversion and qualified nuclear-services capacity, but financial materiality must be tested because the company is larger and diversified.

LTBR is a small-cap speculative shadow candidate for advanced fuel fabrication; survival to Layer 2 requires evidence beyond FEED studies, including licensing, fuel qualification, financing, and customer commitments.

ASPI is an underfollowed/speculative isotope-enrichment optionality name; require independent validation of Quantum Leap Energy’s HALEU technology, NRC path, funding, and binding offtake before upgrading.

Need a separate non-US or OTC mapping for Silex Systems/GLE, Orano, Urenco, Framatome, Westinghouse, and General Matter because several key bottleneck assets are private, foreign-listed, state-owned, or only indirectly accessible through US-listed companies.

The investable chokepoint should be tracked by segment: conversion, enrichment/SWU, HALEU enrichment, deconversion, transport/storage, and qualified fuel fabrication; do not treat uranium miners as interchangeable with fuel-cycle processors.
LEU should remain the primary U.S.-listed public candidate for domestic HALEU/enrichment exposure, but survival to later layers requires DOE task-order and commercial offtake verification.
XE is newly U.S.-listed and should be tracked as a fuel-fabrication chokepoint candidate, not only as an SMR/reactor developer, because TRISO-X has an NRC Part 70 HALEU fuel-fabrication license.
ASPI is a speculative shadow candidate only; keep it in Layer 1B because of possible HALEU enrichment optionality, but require NRC/DOE/customer evidence before upgrading.

For this node, separate mining, conversion, enrichment, deconversion, and fuel fabrication. Cameco is useful as a conversion/fuel-services reference even though it is too large and high-attention for the underfollowed lane.

Potential omitted public names for a follow-up pass: BWXT for TRISO/deconversion/fuel fabrication and Silex/GLE via non-standard or OTC/Australia exposure; verify U.S.-listed accessibility and purity before adding.
LEU is the highest-priority direct public candidate for U.S. HALEU/enrichment exposure because DOE-backed expansion and prior first-HALEU production are directly tied to the node.
XE should be tracked as a newly listed fuel-fabrication/advanced-reactor hybrid; market may focus on SMR deployments while TRISO-X fuel fabrication is the more node-specific chokepoint.
ASPI belongs only in speculative_shadow until licensing, demonstrated scalable enrichment, financing, and TerraPower contract economics are independently verified.

BWXT/Nuclear Fuel Services may be a relevant deconversion/fuel-fabrication candidate but was not included due to the four-candidate cap; next pass should check DOE deconversion awards, naval fuel exposure, and commercial HALEU relevance.

Separate uranium miners from conversion, enrichment, HALEU production, deconversion, and fuel fabrication in future scoring; treating all uranium equities as interchangeable would dilute the bottleneck signal.
For grid_services_epc_labor, use PWR as the reference benchmark for scale, backlog, and craft-skilled execution capacity.
MYRG is a high-purity underfollowed candidate for transmission, distribution, substation, testing, commissioning, and utility-service execution exposure.
PRIM is a mixed-infrastructure but directly relevant utility power-delivery contractor; verify electric T&D purity and recent margin volatility before later-layer promotion.

WLDN is a smaller engineering/technical-services candidate for the interconnection, utility-program, substation-development, and data-center electrical-infrastructure side of the labor/execution chokepoint.

Need a later Layer 2 evidence pass on backlog quality, fixed-price contract exposure, labor availability, union/non-union crew constraints, utility customer concentration, and margin sensitivity to wage inflation across MYRG, PRIM, and WLDN.
For grid_services_epc_labor, keep PWR as the high-attention reference benchmark, not the main alpha target.
MYRG is a direct mid-cap specialty electrical contractor candidate with transmission, distribution, substation, and electrification backlog relevance.
PRIM is a mixed-label infrastructure contractor with utility power-delivery exposure; validate margin quality and backlog mix before elevating.
WLDN is an underfollowed engineering/interconnection candidate after APG acquisition; verify whether APG creates material exposure to data-center substations and grid interconnection.

The investable bottleneck for this node is not only construction backlog but skilled labor availability, large-project execution margins, permitting cadence, and ability to convert MSAs/backlog into profitable revenue.

Potential future searches should examine electrical testing/commissioning, vegetation management, utility inspection, geospatial routing, and specialty line hardware separately; these were not fully covered in this 4-candidate pass.
Use PWR as the benchmark reference name for grid-services/EPC/labor-capacity evidence patterns, not as the main underfollowed discovery target.
MYRG is a high-priority underfollowed candidate for T&D construction exposure, with key diligence around backlog mix, clean-energy project execution history, and labor/productivity sensitivity.
PRIM is a diversified contractor where the grid signal may be hidden inside Utilities power delivery, MSA backlog, and storm-restoration volatility.
WLDN is a lower-attention engineering/interconnection hypothesis; it requires materiality verification for substation, grid-interconnection, and data-center electrical-engineering work.
Need a follow-up pass for pure testing, commissioning, inspection, NETA electrical testing, vegetation management, and regional utility subcontractors; public-company mapping remains incomplete.
The falsification plan for this node should focus on whether project delays are driven by permitting/regulatory bottlenecks or equipment lead times rather than labor/EPC execution scarcity.
MYRG should be retained as a high-priority underfollowed grid-services candidate because it is a specialty electrical contractor with direct T&D and substation exposure.
PRIM should be retained as an underfollowed utility-services candidate; key later-layer work is to separate power-delivery upside from broader energy, gas, communications, and MSA backlog noise.

For grid_services_epc_labor, the critical evidence fields are segment backlog, fixed versus MSA backlog, labor availability, gross margin under wage inflation, substation/transmission mix, and project execution risk.

Testing, commissioning, inspection, and grid-specific engineering providers remain less mapped than construction contractors; future Layer 1B passes should search NV5, Tetra Tech, TRC-like assets if public, and niche electrical testing providers.
GEV should remain the reference leader for gas turbines and utility-scale dispatchable power equipment, but not the core underfollowed discovery target.
GNRC is a direct backup-generation candidate whose data-center relevance needs validation through large-generator backlog, capacity, and customer evidence.
POWL is a strong balance-of-plant electrical infrastructure candidate because of direct data-center order evidence and utility/oil-and-gas market exposure.
CECO is a speculative-shadow candidate for emissions-control and engineered systems tied to fossil power generation; require end-market revenue and backlog verification before promotion.

Need a separate component-supplier search for valves, fuel systems, compressors, heat exchangers, controls, HRSGs, and turbine aftermarket suppliers; this pass only established the first direct universe.
Use GEV only as the reference anchor for the gas-turbine slot bottleneck; avoid letting it crowd out balance-of-plant discovery candidates in later layers.
POWL should be tracked as a direct behind-the-meter generation balance-of-plant candidate because its 2026 disclosure ties a $400M+ data-center order to on-site generation assets.

GNRC belongs in the backup-power lane; key survival test is whether hyperscale/data-center backlog becomes a durable C&I growth engine rather than a temporary supplement to residential storm-cycle demand.

Need a later pass on component suppliers to turbine OEMs: valves, fuel systems, controls, compressors, castings/forgings, heat-recovery steam generators, and turbine aftermarket parts. This pass found stronger public evidence in packaged electrical gear and backup generation than in pure turbine subcomponents.

POWL should be tracked as an underfollowed balance-of-plant electrical-infrastructure supplier for behind-the-meter data-center power and dispatchable-generation projects; verify backlog mix and margin durability.
CECO is a strong underfollowed candidate for gas-power compliance systems; recent natural-gas-power order evidence suggests emissions, acoustic and thermal compliance may be a project gate.
GHM belongs in speculative shadow for niche heat-transfer, vacuum, fluid and power-production systems; keep only if order-level energy/process or power-generation evidence improves.

For this node, the most interesting second-order public-market mappings are not only turbine OEMs but medium-voltage switchgear, engineered power-control buildings, gas-turbine inlet/exhaust systems, emissions/noise compliance, heat-transfer and aftermarket service.

Need a follow-up search specifically for US-listed generator-set enclosure, fuel-system, compressor, valve, controls, SCR/catalyst, heat-recovery steam generator and turbine-service suppliers with market caps between $300M and $10B.

PSIX should remain in the underfollowed lane for dispatchable/backup power because company evidence directly links power-systems growth, data-center demand, manufacturing-capacity expansion, and complete standby/prime/microgrid power systems.

CECO is a strong second-order balance-of-plant candidate: the evidence is not turbine-OEM exposure but power-generation engineered systems, emissions/exhaust/compliance adjacency, record backlog, and a major datacenter-powergen order.

GHM is a speculative-shadow candidate; keep only if later evidence shows material commercial power-generation, SMR, geothermal, hydrogen, or heat-transfer orders rather than mostly defense/space backlog.
GEV’s gas-turbine backlog and data-center electrification orders provide a high-attention reference anchor for the node; use it to test whether smaller suppliers show derivative order acceleration.

Next pass should search named component suppliers to gas-turbine OEMs and data-center generator packagers: valves, controls, fuel systems, silencers/exhaust, SCR/DeNOx, heat exchangers, switchgear interconnect, and field-service contractors.

Energy theme should be split into electricity-demand growth, grid buildout, power equipment, dispatchable generation, gas infrastructure, storage, renewables interconnection, and nuclear fuel-cycle nodes rather than treated as a single commodity-energy trade.

Highest-priority bottleneck candidates for further Serenity layers: HALEU/enrichment, transformers and power-quality equipment, specialty T&D construction labor, grid-stability systems, utility-qualified transmission hardware, and medium-voltage switchgear/control buildings.

Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in utility specifications, certification/requalification gates, testing and diagnostics, environmental compliance systems, and electrical distribution channels.
FERC Order No. 1920 implementation is a core policy catalyst for transmission planning and related equipment/labor nodes.
DOE HALEU task orders and HALEU Availability Program milestones are core catalysts for nuclear fuel-cycle bottleneck validation.

Need company-level filing checks for PLPC, AMSC, ESE, MYRG, CECO, POWL, HUBB, HPS/HMDPF and other candidates to verify revenue exposure, backlog, customer concentration, margin expansion, capacity constraints and whether demand is recurring rather than one-off.

Need to distinguish high-attention reference leaders such as large utilities, IPPs, turbine OEMs and mega-cap electrification suppliers from underfollowed suppliers whose exposure is purer but less obvious.

Need regional power-market evidence by RTO/ISO, especially PJM, ERCOT, MISO and SPP, to identify where data-center load growth is actually constrained by interconnection, transmission, generation capacity or local gas deliverability.

PLPC should be tracked as an underfollowed transmission hardware relationship rather than a generic electrification stock; the main evidence gate is utility qualification/specification presence in high-voltage transmission and reconductoring projects.
AMSC should be tracked as a grid-stability and power-quality relationship; survival to later layers requires current D-VAR/Gridtec revenue, backlog, order cadence and margin evidence.

LEU should be tracked as the cleanest U.S.-listed nuclear enrichment/HALEU chokepoint relationship in this chunk, but execution, DOE funding conversion and legacy supply-transition risk are critical falsification gates.

XE should be tracked as both an advanced-reactor developer and potential TRISO/HALEU fuel-fabrication bottleneck participant; licensing, facility completion, feedstock supply and customer funding must be verified.

ESE should be tracked as a utility diagnostics/testing gatekeeper rather than a headline transformer producer; Megger/Doble integration and Utility Solutions segment acceleration are the key evidence gates.
HMDPF should be tracked as a North American dry-type transformer and power-quality relationship with potential data-center and industrial electrification exposure; channel purity must be verified.

MYRG should be tracked as an underfollowed grid-construction labor and execution relationship, with Quanta as the reference leader; backlog mix, MSAs and labor-margin pressure are the key evidence gates.
HUBB should be treated as a reference leader for utility component demand and pricing rather than the primary underfollowed alpha lane due to its larger-cap status and broader attention.

CECO is a speculative second-order gas-power balance-of-plant relationship; it should not survive without evidence of repeatable power-generation or data-center-adjacent orders and attractive margin structure.

Current Layer 2B evidence is still weakly sourced for company-specific relationships. Next layer should prioritize primary documents: SEC/SEDAR filings, company presentations, product catalogs, DOE/NRC/FERC records, utility approved-vendor lists, RTO project filings, backlog disclosures and earnings-call transcripts.

Do not infer underfollowed status solely from Substack or social-media framing. Validate market cap, analyst coverage, institutional ownership, segment purity and revenue materiality before promoting any candidate.

For the Energy theme, use PWR and VRT as reference anchors for grid execution and data-center power infrastructure, but do not let them crowd out smaller suppliers in transmission hardware, power packages, magnetics, conduit, engineering services and nuclear fuel-cycle chokepoints.
PSIX, GNRC and similar backup-power names should be evaluated through large-load, C&I and data-center backlog quality rather than residential generator narratives alone.

BELFB and NVT are second-order electrical-component mappings; their survival into later layers requires proof of customer pull from AI/data-center, utility T&D, substation, power-quality or standards-driven applications.

PLPC is a potentially important underfollowed transmission hardware candidate, but current evidence is mostly discovery-level external commentary. Prioritize primary-source validation of product qualification, utility approved-material-list presence, backlog and U.S. transmission exposure.

LEU maps to the nuclear enrichment and HALEU chokepoint, but should remain speculative_shadow until DOE task orders, NRC licensing, commercial volumes, financing and Russian-supply transition risks are validated from primary sources.

Need current market cap, analyst coverage, revenue segment, backlog, book-to-bill, customer concentration and margin bridge for each candidate before assigning underfollowed status with high confidence.

Need primary-source company filings and transcripts for PSIX, WLDN, BELFB, NVT, GNRC, ATKR, PLPC and LEU. Current Layer 2B relationships are mostly hypotheses or inferences derived from Layer 1 candidate mappings plus broad FERC/EIA/DOE demand evidence.

Need falsification checks for each node: data-center interconnection delays turning into cancellations, utility capex slippage, component overcapacity, margin compression from labor/material costs, customer insourcing, failed qualification, or stock rerating ahead of fundamentals.
BWXT should remain in the reference lane for nuclear fuel-cycle bottlenecks, but only as an inference until primary filings or DOE contract data show HALEU/deconversion/feedstock materiality.

GHM is a speculative shadow candidate for dispatchable-power and SMR balance-of-plant; survival to Layer 3 requires proof of material energy-generation orders rather than defense/space-driven backlog.
LTBR is best treated as a development-stage downstream advanced-fuel option, not a current infrastructure chokepoint owner.
ASPI has high thematic fit to isotope/enrichment scarcity but very low evidence quality until licensing, technical scale-up and commercial contract economics are validated.
MTZ maps to utility EPC and execution capacity, but it is a diversified reference name; segment backlog and margin mix must be checked before treating it as a grid bottleneck beneficiary.
PPSI is a micro-cap speculative candidate for packaged switchgear, transformer-integrated distribution and microgrid power, requiring strict balance-sheet, capacity and order-quality verification.
ESP should remain a low-confidence speculative magnetics/power-conversion shadow candidate unless commercial grid, data-center, energy-storage or microgrid customer exposure is found.

Need primary-source company filings, earnings transcripts, investor presentations and contract announcements for every ticker in this chunk; the supplied evidence mainly supports theme-level bottlenecks, not company-level revenue materiality.
Need current market-cap, revenue segment, backlog, customer concentration and analyst-coverage data before final underfollowed classification, especially for PPSI, ESP, GHM, LTBR and ASPI.
Need reference-company comparison against LEU for enrichment/HALEU, PLPC for transmission hardware, and established grid/EPC names for MTZ before ranking this chunk in the broader Energy funnel.
